transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Well, I guess I’m here because... honestly, it’s just been going on for a really long time now. Like, for the last couple of years, I just feel so low. All the time. And it’s not just a bad day here and there, you know? It’s like this constant, heavy, empty feeling that just sits right in my chest and it never really lifts. 

I work as a quality inspector—sorting and weighing parts on the line—and I took some college classes a bit ago, but even when I’m at work, just standing there doing my job, I feel it. And it’s not just at work where I'm distracted, it’s everywhere. Even when I’m at church on Sundays, which is supposed to be uplifting, or when I’m around people I actually care about... I’ll just be sitting there with them, and everyone else is fine and talking, but I just have this overwhelming emptiness inside. It’s like I’ve been carrying around this heavy weight for two whole years, and I keep waiting for it to go away, but it just doesn't. I don't know why it won't stop, but it's just always there, dragging me down no matter where I am or who I'm with...
Do you still find pleasure in activities that you used to enjoy?

Not really... no. Not at all, honestly. It’s like... things I used to genuinely love just feel like these giant mountains I have to climb, so I just don't do them anymore. 

Like, I used to play basketball a lot, just pick-up games, but I really enjoyed it. And I’d go to these dance nights with my friends. We used to go all the time, and it was so fun to just get ready and let loose. But I’ve mostly stopped showing up for all of that. My friends will text me to come out to a dance night or a game and I just stare at my phone. I can't bring myself to care. And... well, there's also this church STEM mentoring program I was volunteering with. Since I took some college classes a while back, I was helping the younger kids with their science and math stuff. I used to care about it so much, I really did. I loved seeing them figure things out. But now? I just don't feel anything when I think about it, so I stopped going to that, too. 

And it’s spilling over into everything, not just my free time. It's really messing up my job. I told you I do quality inspection, right? Well, I’ve actually gotten written warnings at work recently. Multiple warnings. Because I’m just... I'm missing shifts entirely because I can't get myself out the door, and when I do go, I'm turning in my inspection documentation late. The paperwork just sits there on my clipboard and I can't bring myself to finish it. My supervisor was getting so frustrated, handing me these official written warnings, and I just stood there. Because how do I explain to him that I can't even find the energy to care about basketball or the kids at church, let alone sorting parts and filling out documentation on time? It just all feels so impossible to keep up with.
Have you noticed any changes in your sleep patterns?

Well, yeah, actually. It’s... it’s been really bad lately, my sleep, I mean. You would think, right, that after being on my feet all day at work—just standing there on the production floor, sorting and weighing those parts for hours on end—that I’d just collapse when I get home. And I am tired. I’m so, so exhausted, like down to my bones. My legs ache, my back aches from leaning over the line. 

But then I actually get into bed, and it’s like... it’s like my brain just refuses to shut off. I pull the covers up, and instead of just drifting off, my mind starts racing. I start thinking about all those written warnings at work, and how I’m probably going to lose my job if I don’t get my documentation in on time, and then I think about the kids at the STEM program and how I just abandoned them, and my friends wondering why I won't go dancing anymore... it just spins and spins. I’ll stare at the ceiling for what feels like hours. And even when I finally do manage to fall asleep, it’s not good sleep. It’s restless. I’ll wake up the next morning when my alarm goes off, and I swear, I feel like I didn’t rest at all. It’s like I just closed my eyes for five minutes. I wake up just as heavy and drained as I was when I laid down, maybe even worse, and then I have to try and drag myself out of bed to go back to the inspection line and do it all over again... it’s just a vicious cycle, you know? I can't catch a break, even when I'm supposed to be resting.
Have you noticed any changes in your appetite?

Yeah, it’s... my eating habits are just a complete mess right now, honestly. It’s like, most days I wake up and I just can’t even think about food. The thought of making something, or even just chewing... nothing sounds good at all. So I go to work on an empty stomach. And then my lunch break rolls around, and I’ll go sit in the break room, and everyone else is microwaving their leftovers and talking, and I just sit there staring at the table. I end up skipping eating entirely until my shift is almost over, just because I have zero desire to put anything in my mouth. 

But then, by the time it gets late in the day, I’m just so incredibly drained from standing on the production floor, and my body finally realizes it hasn't had fuel. But I don't have the energy to get a real meal or even pack one beforehand. So I just... I end up wandering over to the vending machines by the loading dock and grabbing whatever junk is in there. Just random snacks, chips or candy bars, late in the shift, just because I’m so exhausted and it's right there in front of me. 

And it’s really starting to mess with my body, too. Because of all this—not eating all day and then just living off vending machine snacks—my weight has been going up and down constantly. It's actually really frustrating because I have these specific heavy-duty work pants I have to wear for the line, and I swear they fit completely different from month to month. Like, one month I have to pull my belt super tight because they're falling off me, and the next month the button is digging into my stomach. It just makes getting dressed in the morning even harder, you know? When you don't even know if your uniform is going to fit right, it just adds to that feeling of not wanting to leave the house at all...
Do you feel like you're moving slower than you used to or having trouble sitting still?

Moving slower? Um... no, I don't think so. Not really. I mean, I know I said I feel incredibly heavy and drained, like I’m just dragging myself everywhere, but my actual movements... they aren't actually slower, I don't think. Once I’m actually at the inspection line—when I finally manage to get there, anyway—my hands still move at the normal speed. Because, you know, when you're sorting and weighing parts all day, there's a very specific rhythm to it. You grab the part off the line, you check it against the visual specs, put it on the scale, log it, and toss it in the right bin. It’s all muscle memory at this point. So I’m still doing all of that at the same pace, I'm not moving in slow motion or anything. My supervisor hasn't complained about my physical speed on the floor, just... you know, the paperwork being late and me not showing up for my shifts. 

And as for having trouble sitting still? No, definitely not. Honestly, if anything, I wish I could just sit still forever. I don't have any kind of nervous energy or anything like that. I'm not pacing around my apartment or tapping my foot or fidgeting. When I finally get to sit down in the break room on my shift, I just kind of sink into the plastic chair and I don't want to move a single muscle. I just stare at the table until I have to get back up. The thought of pacing or not being able to sit still just sounds completely exhausting to me right now. So, yeah, my body movements are pretty much exactly the same as they’ve always been, I just... I just have absolutely zero energy behind them, if that makes sense.
Do you often feel guilty or worthless about things you've done or haven't done?

Guilty? Or worthless? Um... I don't know, I guess... I mean, I feel bad about missing work and letting people down, like I said before about the STEM program and my friends, but... I don't know if I'd say I feel worthless. It's more just... I'm just so tired. Like, I know I should be doing better, I know I should be getting my paperwork in on time so I don't get those written warnings, and I know I should be showing up for my shifts instead of calling out because I can't drag myself out of bed. And yeah, I feel bad about it, because I know it puts a strain on the rest of the team on the production floor when they're short-staffed and have to cover my line. But I don't sit around thinking I'm a terrible person or that I don't deserve to be here or anything like that. 

It's just... I just don't have the energy to care as much as I probably should, if I'm being completely honest. It's not this deep, crushing guilt that keeps me up at night—well, I mean, I am up at night, like I told you, but it's more just my mind racing about the practical consequences, like losing my job and how I'm going to pay rent, rather than me beating myself up and thinking I'm worthless. I know I'm capable of doing the job, I know I'm a good inspector when I'm actually functioning normally. It's just that right now, everything is so overwhelming and I just can't seem to get it together. So, no, I wouldn't say I feel worthless. Just... really, really overwhelmed and exhausted by everything I'm failing to keep up with.
How long have you been feeling this low and disconnected from things you used to enjoy?

How long? Oh, wow. Um... it feels like forever, honestly, but if I really sit and think about it... it's been about two years and four months. Yeah, two years and four months exactly. I know that sounds weirdly specific, but I remember it because that was right around the time I had to drop out of my community college classes. I was trying to get my associate's degree, you know? Taking a few classes at a time, mostly in the evenings. But then my hours at the plant got changed, and they started needing me on the floor for longer shifts, and the money was just getting so tight... I couldn't afford the tuition and the books anymore, and I definitely couldn't balance the homework with being on my feet inspecting parts for ten hours a day. 

So I had to make the call to stop going to school. And I told myself it was just temporary, just for a semester or two until I saved up some money, but... well, you know how that goes. The weeks just kind of blurred into months, and I never went back. And that’s when this whole heavy, exhausted, empty feeling really started to settle in. Like, before that, even when work was hard, I had school to look forward to, I had a goal I was working toward. But once I stopped taking those classes, it was just... wake up, go to the plant, sort parts, come home, crash. Over and over and over. For two years and four months. It’s like someone just turned the color down on my whole life right then, and it’s just been this endless gray stretch ever since. So, yeah, that's when it all started. Right when I had to give up on those classes.
Have you ever thought about harming yourself or wished you weren't alive during these past two years?

Harming myself? Wished I wasn't alive? Um... no. No, I haven't. I mean, I know I just talked about how everything feels like this endless gray stretch and how exhausted I am all the time, and I know that probably sounds really bleak, but... I don't actually want to die or anything like that. I've never thought about hurting myself. 

It's more just... I wish I could just hit a pause button on everything, you know? Like, I wish I could just go to sleep for a really, really long time and wake up when things are easier, or when I finally have the energy to deal with the written warnings from my supervisor and the rent and the fact that I'm not in school anymore. But that's not the same as wanting to not be alive, right? I just want the pressure to stop. I just want to not feel so heavy all the time. 

I remember when I first had to drop my classes, there was this one night where I was just lying in bed, staring at the ceiling, and I was so overwhelmed by the thought of going into the plant the next morning to just... weigh and sort parts for another ten hours. And I thought, "I just can't do this anymore." But I didn't mean I couldn't do *life* anymore, I just meant I couldn't do the routine. I couldn't do the endless cycle of it. I've never actually sat there and made a plan to hurt myself or thought that the world would be better off without me or anything extreme like that. 

Even when I'm lying awake at 3 AM worrying about losing my job because I can't seem to get out of bed, my brain is always trying to figure out how to fix it—like, how to scrape together the rent, or how to explain my absences to HR—not how to end it all. So, yeah, no thoughts of self-harm. Just... a really strong desire to just hibernate for a few months until I feel like a normal person again, if that makes any sense.
Have you experienced any significant weight loss or gain over the past two years?

Weight loss or gain? Um... yeah, actually. It's been really erratic, to be honest. I mean, it's not like I've dropped or gained fifty pounds all at once, but my weight has definitely been up and down quite a bit over these past two years. It fluctuates enough that I really notice it with my work pants. Like, some months I have to pull my belt as tight as it goes just to keep them up, and then a month or two later, they're uncomfortably tight around the waist and I'm struggling to button them. 

It really just depends on how my eating habits are going, which... well, they're a mess, just like everything else. Most days, especially when I'm scheduled for a long shift at the plant, I just don't have an appetite at all. I'll wake up—barely—and the thought of making breakfast or packing a lunch just feels like climbing a mountain. So I just skip it. I'll go almost my entire shift without eating a single thing because nothing sounds good, and honestly, I just don't have the energy to chew and swallow. I know that sounds ridiculous, but it's true. 

But then, on the flip side, there are times when I'm just so drained and exhausted, usually toward the end of my shift or when I finally get home, and I haven't eaten all day, and suddenly I'm just ravenous. But I still don't have the energy to cook a real meal. So I end up just grabbing whatever is easiest. Like, I'll hit the vending machines in the breakroom and just buy two bags of chips and a candy bar, or I'll stop at a drive-thru on the way home and order way too much food just because it's fast and I don't have to think about it. And then I just eat it all because I'm so depleted. 

So it's this constant cycle of starving myself because I don't care about food, and then bingeing on junk because I'm desperate for energy. And my body just doesn't know what to do with it, I guess. So yeah, my weight has been all over the place. It's just another thing I can't seem to get a handle on. I used to be pretty consistent, back when I was in school and actually had a routine, I'd meal prep on Sundays and everything. But now? Now it's just a complete toss-up whether my uniform is going to fit me from one week to the next.
Do you feel like you're restless or have an inability to sit still when you're not at work?

Restless? Inability to sit still? Oh, gosh, no. No, it's actually the exact opposite of that. If anything, I sit *too* still. When I'm not at the plant... honestly, the second I walk through the door of my apartment, it's like all the strings holding me up just get cut. I don't pace around or fidget or feel like I need to be doing things. I usually just drop my keys on the little table by the door—well, sometimes I don't even make it to the table, they just end up on the floor—and I go straight to the couch or my bed. And I just sit there. Sometimes for hours. 

Like, last weekend, I had a Saturday off, which is rare because they've been pushing so much mandatory overtime lately with the supply chain issues they keep talking about in the morning meetings. But I actually had a day off. And I woke up at maybe 11 AM, and I moved to the living room, sat on the couch, and I swear I didn't move again until it was getting dark outside. I didn't even turn the TV on. I just sat there, staring at the wall, feeling like my limbs were made of lead. 

It takes so much effort just to exist at work, you know? Standing there, inspecting those little metal brackets as they come down the line, flipping them over, checking the welds, weighing them, sorting the defective ones into the red bins... it takes every single ounce of focus and physical energy I have just to keep up with the quota. By the time I get home, my body is just completely done. 

So, no, I don't feel restless at all. I don't have that nervous energy where I need to be moving or doing something. I actually wish I had a little bit of that, to be honest. Like, maybe if I had just a tiny bit of restless energy, I could finally get up and do my laundry, or wash the dishes that have been piling up in the sink for two weeks, or even just take a shower without it feeling like a massive chore. But no, there's no restlessness. I just... I just sink into the furniture and stay there until I absolutely have to get up again.
Do you think your movements or reactions have slowed down compared to how they used to be?

Slowed down? Like... moving in slow motion? Um, no, I don't think so. I mean, I know I just went on and on about how heavy my limbs feel and how I just sit on the couch for hours, so I get why you'd ask that, but... no, my actual physical movements aren't any slower than they used to be. When I actually have to do something, I can do it at a normal speed. 

Like at the plant, the conveyor belt doesn't care how exhausted I am, you know? It just keeps running at the exact same pace. The parts keep coming down the line, and I have to grab them, check the welds, weigh them, and toss them in the right bins. If my reactions were actually slower, or if my hands were moving slower, I'd miss half the parts and they'd just pile up at the end of the belt, and my supervisor would be all over me. I mean, I already get enough grief from him about calling out, so I definitely can't afford to mess up my quota or let defective pieces slip by when I'm actually standing there. So, yeah, I can still keep up with the physical pace just fine. 

It's more just... the amount of mental effort it takes to force my body to move at that normal speed is what's changed. Like, back when I was taking classes, I could just jump out of bed, grab my backpack, and walk across campus without even thinking about it. Now, the thought of getting out of bed feels like I'm trying to move underwater, but once I'm actually up and walking to my car, I'm walking at a normal pace. I'm not, like, shuffling around or talking super slow or anything like that. It just feels like my battery is at one percent while I'm doing it. 

But the actual speed of my movements? No, that hasn't changed. If someone drops something, I still flinch or reach for it just as fast as I used to. I'm pretty sure I react to things exactly the same way I always have, I just... I guess I just dread having to make the movements in the first place. But once I'm moving, I'm moving normally.
Have you experienced any periods of even slight improvement in your mood over the past two years?

Improvement? Um... no. No, not really. I've been trying to think if there was a time, like maybe a good day or even just a good afternoon, but honestly... no. That's actually the main reason I'm here talking to you today. Because for the last couple of years, I just feel low all the time. It's just constant. 

Like, I keep waiting for it to break, you know? For the clouds to part or whatever people say happens, but it just stays exactly the same. I'll be at work—which I already told you is just completely draining—and it's just this heavy feeling sitting right on my chest while I'm sorting parts. But it’s not just work. Even when I'm in places where I'm supposed to feel good, it doesn't change. Like when I go to church... I used to really like going to church. The music, the community, seeing the same familiar faces every Sunday. I kept going even when I started my college classes a while back. But now, on the rare Sundays I actually manage to drag myself out of bed and sit in the pew, I just feel completely disconnected. I'm surrounded by people singing and smiling and greeting each other, and I just feel... well, this really heavy, empty feeling. 

And it's the exact same way when I'm around people I care about, too. My friends will invite me over, or my family will have a get-together for a birthday or a holiday or something, and I might force myself to go because I feel incredibly guilty if I keep flaking on them. But even when I'm sitting right there in the middle of a room full of people I love, people who are laughing and joking and having a genuinely good time, that low feeling just doesn't lift. Not even a little bit. It's like there's this thick, invisible wall between me and everyone else in the room. They're actually experiencing life, and I'm just sort of... trapped under this wet blanket that never, ever dries out. 

So, no, there haven't been any periods where it gets better or lighter. It's just been this continuous, unbroken stretch of feeling incredibly low and empty for two whole years now. It never takes a break, no matter where I am or who I'm with.
Have you had any periods where your low mood was slightly worse than usual over the past two years?

Worse than usual? Um... honestly, I don't think so. It's hard to explain, but it's like... it's just this one, continuous, flat line. Like I was just saying about how it never gets better, it also doesn't really plunge any deeper, either. It's just stuck. 

I mean, you would think there would be days where it gets worse, right? Because bad things still happen. Like, just last month, my supervisor—Dave, he's the one who's always on my case about calling out—he actually wrote me up because I missed a whole batch of defective brackets. They had these tiny, tiny hairline fractures in the welds that you can barely see unless the overhead factory light hits them just perfectly, and my eyes were just so blurry from staring at the conveyor belt for nine hours straight. He pulled me into that little glass office they have on the factory floor and just completely laid into me about quotas and quality control and how the supply chain is already a nightmare without me letting bad parts slip through. 

And you'd think a day like that would make my mood drop, right? Like, you'd expect me to go home and cry, or feel even more depressed than I usually do, or just feel some kind of sharp spike in how terrible everything is. But I didn't. I didn't feel worse at all. I just felt the exact same amount of heavy and empty that I felt the day before, and the day before that. 

It's like... it's like I'm already at the absolute bottom of a swimming pool, you know? You can't sink any lower when you're already lying flat on the concrete at the deep end. There's nowhere else to go. So, no, there aren't really periods where it gets worse or dips down. It's just a constant, heavy feeling that never changes volume. It's always dialed in at the exact same level. Whether it's a Sunday at church, or whether I'm getting screamed at by Dave over metal brackets, or whether I'm just sitting alone on my couch staring at the wall... it's just the exact same shade of gray. Two whole years of just exactly this, day in and day out, without any real change in either direction.
Do you often feel worthless or like you're a burden to others?

Worthless? Um... no, not really. I mean, I know I was just talking about Dave yelling at me and how I call out of work sometimes, and how I feel guilty when I flake on my family, so I can see why you might think I'd be sitting around feeling bad about myself. But it's not really like that. 

I don't think I'm useless. Like, at the plant, I know I'm actually a really good inspector when my eyes aren't completely crossing from staring at the belt. I know how to calibrate the scales, I know the exact tolerance levels for all the different welds, and I know I'm capable of doing the job. I'm a smart person—I mean, I was doing pretty well in my college classes before I had to take a step back. So I know I have worth. I don't sit on the couch thinking, you know, "I'm a terrible person" or "I'm no good at anything." It's not a self-esteem thing at all. 

And as for being a burden... no, I don't think I feel like that either. I pay my own bills, I manage my own life, mostly. I'm not asking my parents or my friends to come over and take care of me or do my laundry or anything like that. When I don't show up to a family get-together, it's not because I think I'm going to ruin their time or because I think I'm dragging everyone down. I know they actually want me there. Like, my mom always makes sure to make that specific potato salad I like whenever they have a barbecue, just in case I actually show up. So I know I matter to them, and I know they care about me. 

That's why I feel guilty when I don't go—because I know they want to see me, not because I think they'd be better off without me. I just literally cannot find the energy to get dressed and drive over there and put on a normal face. But I don't hate myself, and I don't think I'm a burden on anyone's life. It's just... I'm just so incredibly drained all the time. The problem isn't how I view myself, it's just this massive weight on top of me that makes it impossible to do anything. So, no, I don't really have those kinds of thoughts.
Have you ever experienced any thoughts or heard any voices that weren't there?

Voices? Um... no. No, definitely not. I mean, I know things can get pretty bleak in my head with just how heavy and draining everything is all the time, like I was just saying, but it's always just... me in there. I don't hear anyone talking to me or, you know, whispering things when I'm alone in my apartment. 

I mean, the factory where I work is incredibly loud, so sometimes when I get home and finally sit down on the couch, my ears will still be ringing for a couple of hours. It's this constant, high-pitched hum because I have to stand right next to the main conveyor motor all day to inspect those brackets, and even with the little orange foam earplugs they give us in the breakroom, the noise just kind of vibrates right through your skull and settles in your jaw. And Dave is always shouting over the machinery to get our attention, so sometimes I feel like I can still hear the echo of the plant when I'm just trying to close my eyes. But that's just regular noise, you know? Just the aftermath of a nine-hour shift of metal clanking against metal. It's definitely not voices or anything that isn't actually real. 

And as for thoughts... no, it's just my own regular thoughts. They're just really repetitive, I guess. Like, I'll just sit there and my brain will go in these endless circles about how exhausted I am, or I'll think about the college classes I had to put on hold and how I'm ever going to finish my degree, and I'll just kind of dwell on how stuck I feel. But it's always just my own inner voice. I don't feel like anyone else is putting thoughts in my head or anything weird like that. 

Honestly, sometimes I wish my brain would just turn off completely for a few hours because being awake and just sitting with this constant, heavy gray feeling is so tiring. But yeah, it's always firmly grounded in reality. It's just me, my own thoughts, and whatever actual sounds are happening around me, like the hum of my refrigerator or the traffic out on the street. So no, nothing like voices or anything that isn't there.
Has your low mood ever lifted, even if only for a short time, over the past two years?

Lifted? Um... no. No, not at all. I mean, I think that's really the main reason I'm here talking to you right now. Because for the last couple of years, I just feel low all the time. And I really do mean *all* the time. You'd think there would be a break, right? Like maybe a few hours where the clouds part or whatever, but... it just doesn't happen. 

Like, I was talking about my family earlier, and how my mom makes that potato salad for the backyard barbecues. Even when I actually do manage to force myself to go, and I'm sitting there on the patio around people I really care about, people who I know love me... it doesn't lift. I'm just sitting there holding a paper plate, feeling this... this heavy, empty feeling that just completely weighs me down. It doesn't matter that it's a nice sunny day or that everyone is laughing. 

And it's the exact same everywhere else. Like at work, even on a rare good day where the conveyor belt isn't jamming up and Dave isn't on my case... or even when I go to church on Sunday. You know, you go to church hoping to feel something uplifting, or peaceful, or just... lighter, I guess? But I just sit there in the wooden pew, listening to the music or the sermon, and I still feel completely hollow. It just doesn't really lift, ever. Not for a weekend, not for an afternoon. It’s just this constant, heavy emptiness that stays with me no matter where I am or who I'm with.
Have you ever experienced any breaks from reality, such as seeing or hearing things that others cannot?

Wait, didn't we... I mean, I know you asked about the voices a few minutes ago, and like I said, definitely not. But seeing things? Or, like, breaks from reality? Um... no. No, nothing like that either. 

I mean, honestly, a break from reality sounds kind of nice right about now, just to get a vacation from how exhausting everything is, but no, I'm stuck right here in the real world 24/7. It's just me and the same gray walls in my apartment, and the same metal brackets at the plant. I don't see anything that isn't actually there. 

I will say, sometimes, like I was telling you before about the factory, if I've been staring at the exact same spot on the conveyor belt for nine hours straight, just looking for those tiny defects in the welds, when I finally look away or go to the breakroom, I'll see, like, the afterimage of the belt moving? You know how it is when you stare at a bright light too long and then you see spots? It's kind of like that, just this ghost motion of the machinery behind my eyelids because my eyes are just so incredibly strained from focusing. But that's just regular eye fatigue, not a... not a break from reality. I know the breakroom table isn't actually moving. 

And I've never seen, I don't know, people who aren't there, or weird shadows, or anything like that. Everything I see and hear is completely normal, it's just... it's all just really, really dull and heavy. So, yeah, no breaks from reality for me. Just the exact same endless reality every single day.
Have you experienced any significant loss of interest or pleasure in activities for more than two weeks?

Loss of interest? I mean... I don't know if I'd call it a loss of interest, exactly, because it's not like I used to be this super passionate person who suddenly stopped caring. It's more like... everything just feels like a chore, you know? Like, I guess I used to enjoy reading. I have all these paperback fantasy novels stacked up on the little wobbly bookshelf by my TV. I used to be able to just get lost in them for hours on a Sunday afternoon, just completely absorbed in these other worlds. But now, I'll pick one up, and I'll read the same paragraph five times, and the words just don't mean anything. It's just ink on a page. And it's not just for two weeks, it's been like this for... well, for as long as this whole heavy feeling has been around. 

And it's the same with my college classes. I mean, I had to put them on hold, like I said, but even before I officially stopped going, I just... I couldn't find the energy to care about the lectures or the assignments. I used to actually like my sociology class, but then it just became this massive mountain I had to climb every Tuesday and Thursday. I'd sit in the back row and just stare at the clock, feeling completely numb to whatever the professor was saying. 

Even little things, like... I used to like baking. Just simple things, like boxed brownies or chocolate chip cookies. I'd do it on a Friday night to unwind after a long week at the plant. The smell of it in the apartment was nice. But I haven't turned my oven on for anything other than a frozen pizza in months. The thought of getting the bowls out, measuring the ingredients, and then having to wash everything afterward... it just exhausts me before I even start. It's not that I actively dislike these things now, it's just that the pleasure I used to get from them is completely gone. It's not moderate, where I'm just, you know, kind of "meh" about my novels but I can still force myself to read a chapter and get something out of it. I literally cannot get anything out of it. The joy is just... it's gone. It's completely evaporated. And it's severe because it impacts my whole life. It's why my apartment is a mess, because I don't care enough to clean it. It's why I dropped my classes, because I didn't care enough to learn. If it was mild or moderate, I feel like I'd still be functioning normally, just maybe a little less enthusiastically. I don't see my friends, I don't have hobbies anymore, I don't do anything that isn't absolutely mandatory for survival. So, yeah, the loss of interest is definitely severe. I'm surrounded by people singing and smiling and greeting each other, and I just feel... well, this really heavy, empty feeling. 

And it's the exact same way when I'm around people I care about, too. My friends will invite me over, or my family will have a get-together for a birthday or a holiday or something, and I might force myself to go because I feel incredibly guilty if I keep flaking on them. But even when I'm sitting right there in the middle of a room full of people I love, people who are laughing and joking and having a genuinely good time, that low feeling just doesn't lift. Not even a little bit. It's like there's this thick, invisible wall between me and everyone else in the room. They're actually experiencing life, and I'm just sort of... trapped under this wet blanket that never, ever dries out. 

So, no, there haven't been any periods where it gets better or lighter. It's just been this continuous, unbroken stretch of feeling incredibly low and empty for two whole years now. It never takes a break, no matter where I am or who I'm with.

doctor.intent: Determine the severity of depressive episode
doctor.question: Have you had any periods where your low mood was slightly worse than usual over the past two years?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking if there were periods where the low mood was worse than usual, which relates to Major Depressive Episodes occurring during Persistent Depressive Disorder (double depression). The symptom profile does not contain an item for this.

patient.answer:
Worse than usual? Um... honestly, I don't think so. It's hard to explain, but it's like... it's just this one, continuous, flat line. Like I was just saying about how it never gets better, it also doesn't really plunge any deeper, either. It's just stuck. 

I mean, you would think there would be days where it gets worse, right? Because bad things still happen. Like, just last month, my supervisor—Dave, he's the one who's always on my case about calling out—he actually wrote me up because I missed a whole batch of defective brackets. They had these tiny, tiny hairline fractures in the welds that you can barely see unless the overhead factory light hits them just perfectly, and my eyes were just so blurry from staring at the conveyor belt for nine hours straight. He pulled me into that little glass office they have on the factory floor and just completely laid into me about quotas and quality control and how the supply chain is already a nightmare without me letting bad parts slip through. 

And you'd think a day like that would make my mood drop, right? Like, you'd expect me to go home and cry, or feel even more depressed than I usually do, or just feel some kind of sharp spike in how terrible everything is. But I didn't. I didn't feel worse at all. I just felt the exact same amount of heavy and empty that I felt the day before, and the day before that. 

It's like... it's like I'm already at the absolute bottom of a swimming pool, you know? You can't sink any lower when you're already lying flat on the concrete at the deep end. There's nowhere else to go. So, no, there aren't really periods where it gets worse or dips down. It's just a constant, heavy feeling that never changes volume. It's always dialed in at the exact same level. Whether it's a Sunday at church, or whether I'm getting screamed at by Dave over metal brackets, or whether I'm just sitting alone on my couch staring at the wall... it's just the exact same shade of gray. Two whole years of just exactly this, day in and day out, without any real change in either direction.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's low mood is accompanied by feelings of worthlessness
doctor.question: Do you often feel worthless or like you're a burden to others?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about feelings of worthlessness or being a burden (guilt/worthlessness), which is not included in my symptom profile.

patient.answer:
Worthless? Um... no, not really. I mean, I know I was just talking about Dave yelling at me and how I call out of work sometimes, and how I feel guilty when I flake on my family, so I can see why you might think I'd be sitting around feeling bad about myself. But it's not really like that. 

I don't think I'm useless. Like, at the plant, I know I'm actually a really good inspector when my eyes aren't completely crossing from staring at the belt. I know how to calibrate the scales, I know the exact tolerance levels for all the different welds, and I know I'm capable of doing the job. I'm a smart person—I mean, I was doing pretty well in my college classes before I had to take a step back. So I know I have worth. I don't sit on the couch thinking, you know, "I'm a terrible person" or "I'm no good at anything." It's not a self-esteem thing at all. 

And as for being a burden... no, I don't think I feel like that either. I pay my own bills, I manage my own life, mostly. I'm not asking my parents or my friends to come over and take care of me or do my laundry or anything like that. When I don't show up to a family get-together, it's not because I think I'm going to ruin their time or because I think I'm dragging everyone down. I know they actually want me there. Like, my mom always makes sure to make that specific potato salad I like whenever they have a barbecue, just in case I actually show up. So I know I matter to them, and I know they care about me. 

That's why I feel guilty when I don't go—because I know they want to see me, not because I think they'd be better off without me. I just literally cannot find the energy to get dressed and drive over there and put on a normal face. But I don't hate myself, and I don't think I'm a burden on anyone's life. It's just... I'm just so incredibly drained all the time. The problem isn't how I view myself, it's just this massive weight on top of me that makes it impossible to do anything. So, no, I don't really have those kinds of thoughts.

doctor.intent: Determine the presence of psychotic symptoms
doctor.question: Have you ever experienced any thoughts or heard any voices that weren't there?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about psychotic symptoms such as hallucinations or delusions, which are not covered in the patient's symptom profile.

patient.answer:
Voices? Um... no. No, definitely not. I mean, I know things can get pretty bleak in my head with just how heavy and draining everything is all the time, like I was just saying, but it's always just... me in there. I don't hear anyone talking to me or, you know, whispering things when I'm alone in my apartment. 

I mean, the factory where I work is incredibly loud, so sometimes when I get home and finally sit down on the couch, my ears will still be ringing for a couple of hours. It's this constant, high-pitched hum because I have to stand right next to the main conveyor motor all day to inspect those brackets, and even with the little orange foam earplugs they give us in the breakroom, the noise just kind of vibrates right through your skull and settles in your jaw. And Dave is always shouting over the machinery to get our attention, so sometimes I feel like I can still hear the echo of the plant when I'm just trying to close my eyes. But that's just regular noise, you know? Just the aftermath of a nine-hour shift of metal clanking against metal. It's definitely not voices or anything that isn't actually real. 

And as for thoughts... no, it's just my own regular thoughts. They're just really repetitive, I guess. Like, I'll just sit there and my brain will go in these endless circles about how exhausted I am, or I'll think about the college classes I had to put on hold and how I'm ever going to finish my degree, and I'll just kind of dwell on how stuck I feel. But it's always just my own inner voice. I don't feel like anyone else is putting thoughts in my head or anything weird like that. 

Honestly, sometimes I wish my brain would just turn off completely for a few hours because being awake and just sitting with this constant, heavy gray feeling is so tiring. But yeah, it's always firmly grounded in reality. It's just me, my own thoughts, and whatever actual sounds are happening around me, like the hum of my refrigerator or the traffic out on the street. So no, nothing like voices or anything that isn't there.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's low mood is persistent and unchanging
doctor.question: Has your low mood ever lifted, even if only for a short time, over the past two years?

target_item.name: Depressed_Mood
target_item.manifestation: I’m here because for the last couple years I just feel low all the time, like even when I’m at work or church or around people I care about, there’s this heavy empty feeling that doesn’t really lift.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking if the low mood has ever lifted, which directly corresponds to the Depressed_Mood symptom where the patient describes a heavy empty feeling that doesn't really lift.

patient.answer:
Lifted? Um... no. No, not at all. I mean, I think that's really the main reason I'm here talking to you right now. Because for the last couple of years, I just feel low all the time. And I really do mean *all* the time. You'd think there would be a break, right? Like maybe a few hours where the clouds part or whatever, but... it just doesn't happen. 

Like, I was talking about my family earlier, and how my mom makes that potato salad for the backyard barbecues. Even when I actually do manage to force myself to go, and I'm sitting there on the patio around people I really care about, people who I know love me... it doesn't lift. I'm just sitting there holding a paper plate, feeling this... this heavy, empty feeling that just completely weighs me down. It doesn't matter that it's a nice sunny day or that everyone is laughing. 

And it's the exact same everywhere else. Like at work, even on a rare good day where the conveyor belt isn't jamming up and Dave isn't on my case... or even when I go to church on Sunday. You know, you go to church hoping to feel something uplifting, or peaceful, or just... lighter, I guess? But I just sit there in the wooden pew, listening to the music or the sermon, and I still feel completely hollow. It just doesn't really lift, ever. Not for a weekend, not for an afternoon. It’s just this constant, heavy emptiness that stays with me no matter where I am or who I'm with.

doctor.intent: Determine the presence of psychotic symptoms
doctor.question: Have you ever experienced any breaks from reality, such as seeing or hearing things that others cannot?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about psychotic symptoms such as hallucinations (seeing or hearing things), which are not covered by any of the items in the symptom profile.

patient.answer:
Wait, didn't we... I mean, I know you asked about the voices a few minutes ago, and like I said, definitely not. But seeing things? Or, like, breaks from reality? Um... no. No, nothing like that either. 

I mean, honestly, a break from reality sounds kind of nice right about now, just to get a vacation from how exhausting everything is, but no, I'm stuck right here in the real world 24/7. It's just me and the same gray walls in my apartment, and the same metal brackets at the plant. I don't see anything that isn't actually there. 

I will say, sometimes, like I was telling you before about the factory, if I've been staring at the exact same spot on the conveyor belt for nine hours straight, just looking for those tiny defects in the welds, when I finally look away or go to the breakroom, I'll see, like, the afterimage of the belt moving? You know how it is when you stare at a bright light too long and then you see spots? It's kind of like that, just this ghost motion of the machinery behind my eyelids because my eyes are just so incredibly strained from focusing. But that's just regular eye fatigue, not a... not a break from reality. I know the breakroom table isn't actually moving. 

And I've never seen, I don't know, people who aren't there, or weird shadows, or anything like that. Everything I see and hear is completely normal, it's just... it's all just really, really dull and heavy. So, yeah, no breaks from reality for me. Just the exact same endless reality every single day.

doctor.intent: Determine the severity of the patient's depressive episode
doctor.question: Have you experienced any significant loss of interest or pleasure in activities for more than two weeks?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about anhedonia (loss of interest or pleasure in activities), which is not included in my symptom profile.

patient.answer:
Loss of interest? I mean... I don't know if I'd call it a loss of interest, exactly, because it's not like I used to be this super passionate person who suddenly stopped caring. It's more like... everything just feels like a chore, you know? Like, I guess I used to enjoy reading. I have all these paperback fantasy novels stacked up on the little wobbly bookshelf by my TV. I used to be able to just get lost in them for hours on a Sunday afternoon, just completely absorbed in these other worlds. But now, I'll pick one up, and I'll read the same paragraph five times, and the words just don't mean anything. It's just ink on a page. And it's not just for two weeks, it's been like this for... well, for as long as this whole heavy feeling has been around. 

And it's the same with my college classes. I mean, I had to put them on hold, like I said, but even before I officially stopped going, I just... I couldn't find the energy to care about the lectures or the assignments. I used to actually like my sociology class, but then it just became this massive mountain I had to climb every Tuesday and Thursday. I'd sit in the back row and just stare at the clock, feeling completely numb to whatever the professor was saying. 

Even little things, like... I used to like baking. Just simple things, like boxed brownies or chocolate chip cookies. I'd do it on a Friday night to unwind after a long week at the plant. The smell of it in the apartment was nice. But I haven't turned my oven on for anything other than a frozen pizza in months. The thought of getting the bowls out, measuring the ingredients, and then having to wash everything afterward... it just exhausts me before I even start. It's not that I actively dislike these things now, it's just that the pleasure I used to get from them is completely gone. It's like the volume has been turned all the way down on anything that used to bring me even a tiny bit of joy. So, I guess, yeah, if that's what you mean by a loss of interest or pleasure, then yes, definitely. But it's been way longer than two weeks. It's just... it's just how my life is now.

doctor.intent: Determine the severity of depressive episode
doctor.question: Do you feel like your low mood is mild, moderate, or severe most of the time?

target_item.name: Depressed_Mood
target_item.manifestation: I’m here because for the last couple years I just feel low all the time, like even when I’m at work or church or around people I care about, there’s this heavy empty feeling that doesn’t really lift.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about the severity of my low mood, which directly relates to the symptom of depressed mood.

patient.answer:
Well, I think... I mean, I don't know exactly how you define those words, like mild or severe, from a medical standpoint, but to me? It feels severe. Like, very severe. I know I already said this, but I really am just here because for the last couple of years, I just feel low all the time. 

And when I say all the time, I really mean it. It's not like a mild thing where I'm just a little bummed out and I can snap out of it if I watch a funny movie or talk to a friend. It's this heavy, empty feeling that just doesn't really lift, ever. It doesn't matter if I'm at work at the plant, standing there sorting parts, or if I'm sitting in church trying to feel some kind of peace, or even if I'm around people I care about, like my family. It's just always there, dragging me down. 

I feel like a mild low mood would be something you could ignore, you know? Like a tiny pebble in your shoe that you just kind of walk on and forget about for a while. But this... this is like carrying a backpack full of bricks everywhere I go. From the minute I wake up and stare at the ceiling in my apartment, to the minute I finally manage to fall asleep, it's just this constant, severe weight. It dictates everything I do, or rather, everything I can't do anymore, like my classes or reading my books. So, yeah, if I have to pick one of those words, it's definitely severe. It just takes over everything.

doctor.intent: Determine the severity of the patient's loss of interest or pleasure
doctor.question: Would you say that your loss of interest in activities is mild, moderate, or severe?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about the severity of my loss of interest (anhedonia), which is not included in my symptom profile.

patient.answer:
Well, I mean... I guess I'd have to say severe for that, too. Because, like I was trying to explain before about the baking and the books, it's not just a little dip in how much I like things. It's a complete wipeout. It's like... imagine you have a favorite food, right? Something you absolutely love, maybe a really good slice of pizza or something. And then one day, you take a bite, and it tastes like cardboard. And you try it again the next day, and it's still cardboard. And it stays cardboard for years. That's what everything feels like to me now. 

It's not moderate, where I'm just, you know, kind of "meh" about my novels but I can still force myself to read a chapter and get something out of it. I literally cannot get anything out of it. The joy is just... it's gone. It's completely evaporated. And it's severe because it impacts my whole life. It's why my apartment is a mess, because I don't care enough to clean it. It's why I dropped my classes, because I didn't care enough to learn. If it was mild or moderate, I feel like I'd still be functioning normally, just maybe a little less enthusiastically. But I'm not functioning normally. I'm just going to the plant, doing my shift, coming home, and staring at the wall until I fall asleep. I don't see my friends, I don't have hobbies anymore, I don't do anything that isn't absolutely mandatory for survival. So, yeah, the loss of interest is definitely severe. It's taken away everything that made me... me, I guess. Everything that made life actually feel like living instead of just existing.
